analysis.one_liner: Blocks Fair Housing Act lawsuits over policies with discriminatory effects unless deliberate intent is proven.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors, never left the House Judiciary Committee, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Fair Housing Act so that a landlord, lender, or insurer could not be sued for a housing practice that falls harder on a protected group — such as racial minorities, families with children, or people with disabilities — unless the person or company actually intended that harm. Under current law, a policy can be challenged if its effect is discriminatory, even without proof of intent. The bill would remove that 'disparate impact' route, leaving only the harder-to-prove standard of deliberate discrimination. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Landlords, mortgage lenders, insurers, and local zoning authorities whose facially neutral policies — minimum income requirements, credit screens, occupancy rules, or exclusionary zoning — fall more heavily on protected groups. They would face far less legal exposure, because challengers would have to prove intentional discrimination rather than show a discriminatory effect.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision stating that nothing in the Fair Housing Act shall be construed to prohibit conduct that produces a disparate impact on a protected class unless the person engaging in that conduct intended that impact [S2][S3].
This would shift the legal standard from effect to intent, protecting businesses and governments from suits over policies whose discriminatory effects they did not intend [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Renters and homebuyers in protected classes who face housing barriers from neutral-seeming policies. Disparate-impact claims are the main legal tool against practices like income thresholds that screen out most tenants of color, or zoning that keeps affordable housing out; without them, most such cases would be impossible to win, and the discriminatory policies could continue with no legal consequence.
analysis.who_pays_short: Renters and buyers facing discriminatory policies

drawbacks.text: A pure intent standard would make most housing discrimination cases unprovable. Discriminatory outcomes often arise from facially neutral policies — credit score cutoffs, criminal-history bans, large-lot zoning — where no one intended to exclude a protected class, so the conduct would be lawful even though the harm falls along racial and other protected lines [S2][S3].

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is that disparate-impact liability can impose real costs on ordinary housing providers for routine, non-discriminatory business decisions, and can push them toward racial quotas or dropping legitimate screening rules to avoid lawsuits. Supporters framed the bill as protecting local control and independence in housing decisions, as its title reflects [S1][S3].
By 2015 the Supreme Court had upheld disparate-impact liability under the Fair Housing Act, so the bill would have overridden that settled reading of the statute by statute [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — shielding landlords, lenders, and local governments from lawsuits over policies they did not intend to be discriminatory — comes at the cost of removing the primary legal remedy available to renters and buyers who face practices that exclude protected groups without any provable intent. Housing discrimination that operates through neutral rules is precisely the kind that an intent standard cannot reach. On balance, the bill's cost to fair-housing enforcement outweighs its benefit to housing providers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and later to its Constitution subcommittee, and it died there when the Congress ended, without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on July 21, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
No member of the House — including no Republican — signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
On September 8, 2015, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, where it stayed [S5].
The committee never held a hearing or advanced the bill, and it expired at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017, without a vote in either chamber [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the disparate-impact tool under the Fair Housing Act survived, which is the better outcome for renters, homebuyers, and civil-rights enforcement; housing providers, lenders, and local zoning authorities are the parties the bill would have benefited, and they remain subject to disparate-impact suits.

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Not one member from either party cosponsored the bill, signaling no appetite to advance it.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote or floor debate to measure party alignment; the bill's zero cosponsors from either party and its death in committee make the partisan shape effectively unknowable, though the sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have freed them from disparate-impact suits over screening policies — income floors, credit and criminal-history rules — that fall harder on protected groups. Their gain comes at the direct cost of tenants' ability to challenge those practices.

Lending and insurance practices are frequent targets of disparate-impact claims; an intent requirement would have sharply reduced their legal exposure while leaving affected borrowers and applicants without a remedy.

Exclusionary zoning is commonly challenged under disparate-impact theory; the bill's stated aim of 'local independence' would have protected those decisions from such suits, keeping affordable housing out of jurisdictions that block it.
